extracted.intended_audience: aspiring novelists and fiction writers preparing opening pages for critique or submission
extracted.subtask_description: Advice for novelists on how to write first chapters/first pages that engage agents, editors, and readers—covering where a story should start, how to handle backstory, testing openings, and critique/submission practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: First pages must grab an editor/agent
rubrics_metrics.description: If an editor or agent isn’t drawn into the story quickly, the chance of them continuing to read is very small.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The submission pile is always huge and a bad first chapter makes it easy to say no. Make that first chapter shine; don’t make it easy for an editor or agent to say no to your book.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid frontloading backstory and character introductions
rubrics_metrics.description: Many first chapters focus too much on back story and character introductions instead of jumping right in to the plot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Overdoing backstory in opening chapters is a common flaw (likened to 'driving a car while watching the rearview mirror'). It can bog down momentum and prevent readers from being hooked.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reveal backstory gradually and naturally (breadcrumbing)
rubrics_metrics.description: It’s great to have a thorough understanding of characters and back story, but you should reveal these details to your audience gradually and naturally as you write.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deliver backstory in 'breadcrumb doses' through the narrative as required to keep the reader engaged rather than all at once in the opening.

rubrics_metrics.name: Start the story where the story actually starts
rubrics_metrics.description: Take an honest look at your WIP: Where does the story actually start? Is your first chapter (or two) necessary to the book?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cut or relocate material that precedes the true inciting action; ensure the opening justifies its place in the manuscript and moves the plot forward.

rubrics_metrics.name: Begin in action / drop the reader into the middle of things
rubrics_metrics.description: Begin your first chapters in action to hook the reader—'drop right into the middle of things' / 'begin in action'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Starting with a moment of action or tension can immediately establish stakes and curiosity. Use in medias res when appropriate to create immediate engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test your first page with unbiased readers
rubrics_metrics.description: Send your first page to five friends/acquaintances and ask them to honestly tell you if they would want to read more based on that first page and why or why not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use short, focused reader tests to learn whether your opening compels continuation and to collect concrete reasons for reactions that you can act on.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rewrite your first chapter after completing the manuscript
rubrics_metrics.description: Write your first chapter and do the best you can. After you finish the last chapter, go back and rewrite the first.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Once the whole story exists, you’ll better know what the opening needs to set up and can rewrite it to align with the finished book’s tone, pacing, and revelations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use critique partners/critique groups for early feedback
rubrics_metrics.description: Critique partners are great at catching problems like too much backstory—please join a critique group if you aren’t in one already.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critique partners spend more time with your work than an agent and can provide detailed, iterative feedback. Trust experienced critique readers while balancing their advice with your vision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer objective/anonymous reading in critique settings
rubrics_metrics.description: Some workshops read students' submissions aloud anonymously (faculty read them) which made it easier to critique really poor submissions and provided dispassionate feedback.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Having someone else read aloud and masking author identity can produce more objective feedback and reduce emotional responses during critique sessions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be constructive and encouraging when critiquing openings
rubrics_metrics.description: Critique accompanied by encouragement is more helpful; public harshness without encouragement can crush writers' confidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When offering critique, strive to be honest but supportive—point out strengths as well as weaknesses to make feedback actionable and to encourage revision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize that a strong authorial voice can compensate
rubrics_metrics.description: Even with too much up-front backstory, readers sometimes keep reading because of the author’s voice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Voice can overcome certain structural problems; if your voice is compelling it may buy you leeway, but don’t rely on voice alone to mask structural issues in the opening.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider genre expectations and audience when pacing the opening
rubrics_metrics.description: Different genres and readers expect different openings (example: cozy mysteries vs. action-driven novels); agents and editors may disagree about pacing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Know your genre’s conventions and the expectations of your target readers and gatekeepers. What counts as 'too slow' in one subgenre may be appropriate in another—use critique partners familiar with your genre.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepare submission materials in the order agents use them (synopsis then sample)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the story sounds interesting from the initial query letter, agents request a proposal; proposals include a synopsis and the first 50 pages. 'I always read the synopsis first.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize a strong query and synopsis—agents often screen by synopsis before reading sample pages—so a compelling synopsis plus a polished first 50 pages is important for formal submissions.
